tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing the pressure monitoring network as a strategic asset.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: permanent logger network covering zones, critical points and boundaries.

cards.label: Define the decisions the monitoring network must support, from control to complaints
Set coverage standards for loggers by zone type and critical location
Audit current coverage, data quality and logger maintenance against the standards
Fund the gaps that affect pressure control and customer investigations
Set data review routines so alarms and trends are acted on weekly
Report network health and the decisions it informed in the annual review

tasks.explanation: Loggers that nobody reads are scrap. Defining the decisions first sets coverage where it matters, and routine review with annual reporting keeps the network a working asset rather than an installation.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adopting a five year water quality strategy for distribution.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering residual, water age, materials, sampling and customer trust.

cards.label: Summarize current quality performance and risks from monitoring and complaint data
Set strategy goals for residual stability, water age and compliance performance
Identify the programs needed for each goal, from turnover to mains renewal
Cost the programs and sequence them within the capital and operating plans
Present the strategy to the board with the risks of deferring each program
Report strategy progress annually with the same measures used to set the goals

tasks.explanation: A quality strategy measured with the same indicators that justified it can be judged fairly. Stating deferral risks at adoption stops programs being quietly cut later without the consequence being seen.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading a distribution water quality risk review at utility level.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual risk review from source changes to customer taps.

cards.label: List quality hazards at each stage, from storage to service lines
Score each hazard for likelihood and consequence using monitoring evidence
Check the controls in place for each high scoring hazard and test their records
Assign improvement actions with owners for hazards where controls are weak
Set the monitoring that will show whether each improvement worked
Report the risk position and actions to the board quality committee

tasks.explanation: Risk review fails when it lists hazards without testing controls. Scoring from evidence, checking control records and assigning monitored improvements turns the register into protection rather than paperwork.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a multiple barrier review of the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review of barriers from treatment handover to storage, mains and backflow control.

cards.label: List the barriers protecting quality at each stage of distribution
Gather performance evidence for each barrier from records and monitoring
Identify stages where a single barrier carries the whole protection
Strengthen weak stages with added controls or monitoring first
Set barrier performance indicators and review them on a fixed cycle
Report barrier status in the annual quality report to leadership

tasks.explanation: Safe water in distribution rests on several barriers working together. Finding the stages where one barrier stands alone, and strengthening those first, is the highest value work the review can direct.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the distribution utility for an emerging contaminant concern.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: readiness plan for a newly discussed substance in the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality review process.

cards.label: Review the available science summary and any guideline direction in plain terms
Check whether current treatment and distribution materials could affect levels
Design a monitoring plan for entry points and representative distribution sites
Prepare customer communication lines that are accurate without causing alarm
Brief leadership on likely scenarios, costs and decision points
Run the monitoring plan and review results against the prepared scenarios

tasks.explanation: Readiness means the utility can answer questions with data when concern arrives. Monitoring designed in advance, with honest communication lines ready, prevents both complacency and panic.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a utility wide water age reduction strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering storage sizing, turnover, dead ends and low use areas.

cards.label: Map water age across the system using the model and residual data
Rank high age areas by quality risk, including residual loss and complaints
Match each area to a remedy, from turnover targets to looping or resizing
Sequence remedies by risk and by alignment with planned renewal work
Set water age and residual targets for each treated area
Verify improvement from residual trends after each remedy is delivered

tasks.explanation: Water age is the root of many quality complaints, so the strategy maps it before prescribing. Matching remedies to renewal work shares excavation costs, and residual trends prove whether age actually fell.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a strategic review of disinfection practice in distribution.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review covering residual targets, booster stations and byproduct balance.

cards.label: Compile residual and byproduct results across zones and seasons
Identify zones where residual is hard to hold and zones where it runs high
Review booster station performance, dosing control and maintenance records
Model residual target options and their byproduct and cost effects
Select zone targets that hold protection with the lowest practical byproduct formation
Implement the targets with a season of enhanced monitoring to confirm the balance

tasks.explanation: Residual strategy is a balance, not a maximum. Zone by zone evidence lets targets protect the far ends of the system without overdosing the near ends, and a monitored first season confirms the balance holds.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing the regulatory sampling program at utility level.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: governance of sampling required under provincial drinking water requirements.

cards.label: Confirm the sampling obligations, sites and frequencies in a controlled schedule
Audit site selection so sites represent zones, storage and high age areas
Set sampler training, chain of custody and transport standards
Review results monthly for missed samples, holding issues and trends
Investigate any adverse or unusual result under the response procedure
Report sampling compliance and result trends to leadership quarterly

tasks.explanation: Sampling is the utility evidence that water is safe, so its governance is a leadership duty. Auditing site representativeness and reviewing compliance monthly catches program drift before a regulator does.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting decision thresholds for water quality incidents.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: framework defining when results trigger investigation, advisory discussion or public notice.

cards.label: List the result types and complaint patterns that could signal an incident
Set investigation thresholds for each type using guideline values and trends
Define who decides on escalation at each threshold, including after hours
Agree the consultation route with the provincial drinking water authority
Document the framework and train duty managers against it
Review thresholds after every incident and near miss for lessons

tasks.explanation: Thresholds decided in calm times protect decision makers in a crisis. Naming who decides, and agreeing the consultation route in advance, removes delay when an unusual result arrives at night.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a consumer confidence and transparency strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering annual reporting, data publication and complaint insight.

cards.label: Analyse what customers ask and complain about from contact records
Publish the annual quality report in plain language with local results
Open a public data summary showing residual and compliance performance by area
Set response standards for quality contacts, including sampling follow up
Feed recurring contact themes into the quality risk review as evidence
Measure trust and understanding in a customer survey and report the change

tasks.explanation: Trust is built by publishing real local results before customers have to ask. Treating contact themes as quality evidence, not just service work, closes the loop between the public and the risk process.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing a pilot of a new distribution quality technology.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: pilot of a new monitoring or treatment technology in one pressure zone.

cards.label: State the problem the technology must solve and the success measures
Select a pilot zone that represents the wider system fairly
Run the pilot through a full seasonal cycle including winter conditions
Compare pilot results with the control zone using the stated measures
Decide adoption, extension or rejection on the recorded evidence
Publish the pilot findings internally so other zones can use them

tasks.explanation: A pilot judged on measures stated in advance cannot be declared a success by enthusiasm. A full seasonal cycle in western conditions, compared with a control zone, gives an adoption decision the utility can defend.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building a distribution performance benchmarking framework.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: framework of indicators for loss, quality, service, asset and cost performance.

cards.label: Select indicators that match the utility strategy and board priorities
Define each indicator precisely, with data source and calculation method
Collect three years of history to set baselines for every indicator
Set targets that stretch performance without inviting data gaming
Report the indicator set quarterly with commentary on movement and causes
Review the framework annually and retire indicators that no longer drive action

tasks.explanation: Indicators only improve performance when definitions are fixed and history is honest. Retiring indicators that drive no action keeps the framework a management tool rather than a report factory.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a peer utility benchmarking comparison that leadership can trust.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: comparison with similar western Canadian utilities on cost and performance.

cards.label: Select peer utilities with similar climate, size and supply arrangements
Agree common definitions for each measure with the peer group
Exchange data under a written protocol covering quality checks
Normalize results for known differences such as frost depth and density
Present gaps with the operational reasons behind them, not rankings alone
Adopt improvement actions from the practices of the strongest peers

tasks.explanation: Raw rankings mislead when climates and definitions differ. Normalizing for frost depth and density, then explaining gaps operationally, turns benchmarking from a league table into learning.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for an energy optimization strategy for the pumping fleet.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering pump efficiency, scheduling, tariffs and renewal choices.

cards.label: Measure energy per cubic metre delivered for each station and pump
Test pump efficiency and compare with original duty curves
Model schedule changes that move pumping into lower tariff periods within storage limits
Rank stations for pump renewal by energy wasted and condition
Implement schedule changes first, then renew pumps in rank order
Report energy per cubic metre monthly against the strategy baseline

tasks.explanation: Schedule changes cost little and save immediately, so they precede capital renewal. A single measure, energy per cubic metre, reported monthly, shows whether the strategy is working station by station.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing the hydraulic model as a utility decision asset.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: governance covering model updates, calibration, access and use in decisions.

cards.label: Set the model update cycle tied to construction completion and demand data
Calibrate the model against field pressure and flow tests on a set program
Record model version, data vintage and known limits with each issue
Require major capacity decisions to cite the model version used
Train planners and operators in what the model can and cannot show
Audit model predictions against built project performance annually

tasks.explanation: A model with unknown vintage produces confident wrong answers. Version control, calibration and an annual audit against real project performance keep the model worthy of the decisions based on it.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a strategy to use SCADA and operational data for optimization.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: data strategy covering alarms, trends, historian quality and analytics use.

cards.label: Inventory the operational data collected and the decisions each data set supports
Fix historian gaps, tag naming and time alignment for the key data sets
Build standard trend reviews for pressure, storage, pumping and residual
Rationalize alarms so operators see the events that need action
Use the cleaned data in monthly optimization reviews with operations leads
Report the operational savings found from data reviews each quarter

tasks.explanation: Analytics on misaligned, gappy data produces noise. Fixing the historian basics first, then building routine trend reviews, is what turns stored data into operating savings.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a strategic review of distribution maintenance practice.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review balancing preventive, predictive and reactive work across asset classes.

cards.label: Analyse work history to split effort between preventive, predictive and reactive jobs
Identify asset classes where reactive work dominates and failure costs are high
Set target maintenance mixes by asset class based on criticality
Move inspection and monitoring resources to the classes below target
Adjust crew skills and spares to match the new maintenance mix
Track failure rates and reactive share quarterly against the targets

tasks.explanation: Reactive dominance is a strategy failure, not a crew failure. Setting target mixes by criticality and moving inspection effort accordingly reduces failures where they cost most.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for redesigning the system flushing program for water and quality efficiency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program redesign covering unidirectional flushing, targeting and water reuse awareness.

cards.label: Map sediment, age and complaint evidence to find where flushing earns its water
Convert priority areas to unidirectional sequences from clean water outward
Set target velocities and volumes for each sequence from pipe data
Schedule sequences to protect residual and avoid peak demand periods
Record water used and quality improvement for every sequence
Review the program annually and retire sequences that show no benefit

tasks.explanation: Flushing everywhere on a calendar wastes water where there is no problem. Evidence based targeting with recorded volumes and results lets the program defend every cubic metre it uses.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for an optimization review of booster disinfection stations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review of dosing control, energy, chemical use and reliability across stations.

cards.label: Compile dose, residual, chemical use and run hours for each station
Compare achieved residual control with the zone target band
Check dosing equipment condition, calibration and chemical storage safety
Model control changes that tighten residual control with less chemical
Implement the best changes and standardize settings across similar stations
Monitor residual stability and chemical use for a season after the changes

tasks.explanation: Booster stations drift individually unless reviewed as a fleet. Comparing control performance station by station finds the outliers, and standardizing proven settings spreads the best practice.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for evaluating a capital option against an operating option for a system problem.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: comparison such as new storage versus revised pump scheduling for a peak problem.

cards.label: Define the service problem and the performance each option must deliver
Develop the capital option and the operating option to comparable detail
Cost both options over the same period, including risk and maintenance
Test both against peak, outage and growth scenarios
Select the option that delivers the service at lower whole life cost and risk
Record the decision basis so future reviewers can see the tradeoff made

tasks.explanation: Operating solutions are often dismissed before they are costed. Developing both options to comparable detail, over the same period and scenarios, gives leadership a genuine choice instead of a foregone conclusion.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing continuous improvement across distribution operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program collecting, testing and scaling improvement ideas from all crews.

cards.label: Invite improvement ideas against the largest cost, loss and quality problems
Screen ideas quickly and select a small number for structured trials
Run trials with before and after measures agreed at the start
Scale the ideas that prove out into standard practice with training
Publish trial results, including the ideas that did not work
Report savings and lessons to leadership quarterly and refresh the idea list

tasks.explanation: Publishing failed trials is what keeps staff offering ideas. Small measured trials, scaled only on evidence, build improvement into routine work instead of leaving it to occasional projects.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the annual distribution operating budget at leadership level.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: budget build covering labour, energy, chemicals, maintenance and programs.

cards.label: Start from service levels and program commitments the budget must fund
Build cost lines from activity volumes and unit costs, not last year plus a percentage
Challenge each line for savings that do not cut service or increase risk
Show the risk and service effect of any saving that is accepted
Balance the budget to the funding available and record the choices made
Present the budget with its service and risk consequences to the board

tasks.explanation: Activity based building exposes what the budget actually buys. Recording the service effect of every accepted saving stops quiet cuts that reappear later as failures.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running a capital budget challenge session for the distribution program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: session where project sponsors defend scope, cost and timing to leadership.

cards.label: Circulate business cases with costs, benefits and deferral risks in advance
Have each sponsor present the need, the options considered and the recommended scope
Challenge scope for gold plating and timing for trigger evidence
Test estimates against recent delivered project costs for similar work
Decide approvals, deferrals and scope changes with reasons recorded
Reissue the capital program reflecting the session decisions

tasks.explanation: Challenge works when cases are read in advance and estimates are tested against real delivered costs. Recorded reasons protect deferred projects from being quietly revived without new evidence.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for developing a rate and funding strategy for the water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering rates, reserves, grants and borrowing for the capital program.

cards.label: Forecast the revenue requirement from operating costs and the capital program
Model funding mixes of rates, reserves, borrowing and available grants
Show the customer bill impact of each mix over ten years
Test each mix for fairness between current and future customers
Recommend the mix that funds the program with stable, explainable bill changes
Adopt the strategy and use it as the basis for annual rate setting

tasks.explanation: Funding choices decide who pays and when, so fairness between generations is tested openly. A strategy adopted once, then used for annual rates, replaces yearly improvisation with a defensible path.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for designing the board performance report for distribution operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: quarterly report covering quality, loss, service, safety, finance and capital delivery.

cards.label: Select the small set of measures the board needs to govern, not just to know
Set each measure with a target, a tolerance band and a data owner
Present trends over two years rather than single period results
Require commentary that explains movement and states corrective actions
Include one deep dive topic per quarter on a rotating risk area
Review the report format annually with the board and prune unused measures

tasks.explanation: Boards govern through trends and tolerances, not data dumps. A rotating deep dive ensures quiet risk areas get board attention before they become incidents.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting a reserve fund policy for the distribution utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: policy covering operating, capital and emergency reserves with target levels.

cards.label: Identify the risks each reserve exists to cover, from revenue shocks to major breaks
Size each reserve from the cost and likelihood of those events
Set target levels and the rules for drawing on and refilling each reserve
Show the rate effect of building reserves to target over a stated period
Approve the policy at board level and report reserve positions quarterly
Review target levels after any major draw or change in risk profile

tasks.explanation: Reserves sized from named risks can be defended to customers and auditors. Draw and refill rules agreed in advance stop reserves becoming either a slush fund or an untouchable hoard.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the procurement strategy for a major multi year program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy for a large mains renewal and metering program delivered over five years.

cards.label: Analyse the market capacity of local contractors and suppliers for the work
Package work into lots sized to attract competition without losing coordination
Choose contract forms that share risk fairly for ground and quantity uncertainty
Build quality and past performance into evaluation alongside price
Set program level reporting on cost, progress and contractor performance
Review the strategy after the first year of delivery and adjust lot sizes

tasks.explanation: Lot size decides who can bid, so it is a competition decision as much as an engineering one. Reviewing the strategy after year one lets real market response correct the assumptions.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a leadership review of internal controls over utility operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: controls covering purchasing, inventory, overtime, billing adjustments and data changes.

cards.label: Map the processes where money, water data or customer accounts can be altered
Identify the control that guards each process and the person who owns it
Test a sample of transactions against the controls for the past year
Grade control gaps by financial and reputational risk
Direct fixes for the highest risk gaps with owners and dates
Report control health to the audit committee annually

tasks.explanation: Controls are tested on real transactions, not on policy documents. Grading gaps by risk and reporting to the audit committee keeps control work focused where failure would hurt most.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for refreshing the distribution policy framework.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review of operating policies covering service, quality, pressure and customer duties.

cards.label: Inventory all current policies with owners and last review dates
Retire policies that duplicate others or describe practice nobody follows
Update retained policies for current standards, roles and systems
Consult operations staff on whether each policy can actually be followed
Approve the refreshed set and publish it in one controlled location
Set a review cycle so no policy ages beyond its review date again

tasks.explanation: A policy that cannot be followed teaches staff to ignore all policies. Testing each policy with the people who must follow it, and retiring dead ones, restores the authority of the set.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a stakeholder engagement strategy for a disruptive renewal program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: multi year program renewing mains through dense commercial and residential streets.

cards.label: Map affected groups, from residents and businesses to emergency services
Identify the impacts each group cares about, from access to water shutoffs
Set engagement methods and notice periods matched to each impact
Give the program a single contact point and a published response standard
Brief local representatives before each construction stage begins
Review complaints and engagement results after each stage and adjust the approach

tasks.explanation: Engagement planned by impact, not by habit, reaches people with what they actually need to know. A single contact point with a response standard turns complaints into managed information instead of escalation.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for updating the twenty year financial plan for the water utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plan linking asset needs, demand scenarios, rates and reserves.

cards.label: Refresh asset renewal needs and capacity projects from the current plans
Apply demand and growth scenarios to revenue and operating cost forecasts
Model rates, reserves and borrowing needed under each scenario
Identify the years where funding pressure peaks under the central scenario
Develop smoothing options for the peak years and state their tradeoffs
Adopt the plan and use it to set the next five years of budgets and rates

tasks.explanation: The long term plan exists to find funding pressure early, while smoothing is still cheap. Adopting it as the basis for budgets connects daily decisions to the twenty year picture.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for establishing governance of the distribution emergency program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program covering plans, roles, training, exercises and plan maintenance.

cards.label: Name an accountable emergency program lead at senior level
Inventory the credible emergency scenarios for this system and climate
Confirm a current plan, trained lead and deputy for each scenario
Set the exercise and plan review calendar for the year
Fund the gaps found in plans, equipment and training
Report program readiness to the board annually with the gaps remaining

tasks.explanation: Emergency readiness fails quietly between incidents, so it needs an owner, a calendar and board reporting like any other program. Funding gaps in calm times is the whole point of governance.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading the utility response to a major supply failure.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: trunk main or source failure cutting supply to a large part of the city.

cards.label: Confirm the scale of the failure from field and control room reports
Activate the emergency structure and name the incident lead and deputies
Protect remaining supply by rezoning, storage control and demand requests
Set public messages on the affected area, expected duration and safe water advice
Direct repair and alternative supply work with safety and quality checks
Stand down in stages as supply is proven, and record the decisions taken

tasks.explanation: Leadership in a supply failure is about protecting what remains while repair proceeds. Staged stand down, only as supply is proven, prevents a second crisis caused by declaring success too early.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for establishing a mutual aid framework with neighbouring utilities.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: framework covering staff, equipment, water supply and cost recovery.

cards.label: Identify the help this utility could need and could offer, by scenario
Agree framework terms with neighbouring utilities before any incident
Record contact points, request routes and decision authority for each party
Set cost recovery, liability and worker safety terms in the agreement
Test the request route in an exercise with a live call to each partner
Review the framework annually and after every activation

tasks.explanation: Mutual aid negotiated during an emergency arrives late and disputed. Terms, contacts and cost rules agreed in advance, then tested with real calls, make aid a phone call instead of a negotiation.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading public communication during a water emergency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: communication for a boil water advisory or major outage affecting many customers.

cards.label: Confirm the facts, the affected area and the protective action required
Approve the first public message within the set time standard for the event type
Issue the message through every channel the affected customers actually use
Set and meet a fixed update rhythm, even when the update is that work continues
Correct any circulating misinformation with clear, sourced statements
Announce the all clear only on confirmed results, with the evidence summarized

tasks.explanation: Silence is filled by rumour, so a fixed update rhythm matters even when nothing has changed. The all clear waits for confirmed results, because trust lost on a premature all clear is not recovered.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for running a board level emergency exercise program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual program of tabletop and live exercises for senior leaders and duty staff.

cards.label: Select scenarios from the risk register, including one severe winter event
Set exercise objectives covering decisions, communication and mutual aid
Brief participants on roles without revealing the scenario developments
Run the exercise with timed developments that force real decisions
Score performance against the objectives with independent observers
Convert findings into owned improvement actions tracked to completion

tasks.explanation: Exercises that reveal the scenario in advance test memory, not readiness. Timed developments and independent scoring produce findings worth acting on, and tracking actions to completion closes the loop.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building the emergency plan for vulnerable customers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plan covering care facilities, dialysis patients, schools and high rise buildings.

cards.label: Identify facilities and customer groups that cannot manage without water
Record their water needs, contact points and internal storage where known
Set priority notification and alternative supply arrangements for each group
Agree roles with health and municipal emergency partners for support
Test notification to every listed facility in an annual exercise
Update the list after every incident and every facility change reported

tasks.explanation: Vulnerable customers cannot queue at a water tanker, so their arrangements are made in advance and tested. An annual notification test finds the changed phone numbers before an emergency does.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing recovery after a major distribution emergency.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: recovery phase covering service restoration, customer redress and system checks.

cards.label: Confirm all customers are restored and water quality is verified across the area
Complete system checks for pressure damage, contamination signs and storage state
Record customer impacts, including vulnerable customers and business losses
Apply the redress policy consistently and publish how customers can claim
Restore emergency stocks, equipment and mutual aid obligations
Close the recovery phase formally with a report to leadership

tasks.explanation: Recovery is part of the emergency, not an afterthought. Formal closure with system checks, consistent redress and restocked resources ensures the utility is ready for the next event, not just finished with this one.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a supply chain continuity plan for critical distribution materials.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plan covering pipe, fittings, valves, chemicals and fuel for emergency work.

cards.label: List the materials and services whose absence would stop emergency repair
Measure current stock and supplier lead times for each critical item
Set minimum stock levels from the largest credible repair scenario
Arrange secondary suppliers or mutual aid sources for single source items
Set stock rotation so emergency material stays usable and in date
Audit stock against the plan twice a year and after every major use

tasks.explanation: The largest credible repair sets the stock level, not average use. Secondary sources for single source items and regular audits keep the plan real rather than a list of good intentions.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading operations during a cyber incident affecting control systems.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: incident where SCADA visibility is lost or cannot be trusted.

cards.label: Confirm the extent of the loss with the control room and technology staff
Move affected stations and zones to safe manual operation under local control
Increase field rounds, pressure checks and manual residual sampling
Isolate affected systems under the direction of the incident technology lead
Inform leadership and the provincial contact as the notification plan requires
Return to normal control only after systems are verified clean and data is validated

tasks.explanation: Manual operation keeps water safe while systems are untrusted, and field verification replaces the missing data. Returning to normal control waits for verified clean systems, not for impatience.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing after action improvement following a major incident.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: process from incident close to verified completion of all lessons.

cards.label: Commission the after action review with an independent facilitator
Gather records, timelines and staff accounts while memory is fresh
Identify findings covering decisions, resources, communication and training
Convert findings into actions with owners, dates and success measures
Track actions at leadership level until each is verified complete
Test the most important fixes in the next emergency exercise

tasks.explanation: Lessons are not learned until they are tested. Tracking actions to verified completion, then exercising the fixes, is what separates an after action process from a report on a shelf.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adopting a utility wide winter operations strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering freeze risk, staffing, materials, communication and budgets.

cards.label: Review the last three winters for failures, costs and customer impacts
Map the assets and areas most exposed to frost and extreme cold
Set winter service standards for response times and customer protection
Fund staffing, materials and contractor support to meet the standards
Publish customer freeze prevention guidance before the cold season
Review the strategy each spring against the winter that just passed

tasks.explanation: Winter strategy built from the last three winters targets the failures that actually repeat. Spring review, while the evidence is fresh, keeps each winter cheaper and safer than the last.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading the utility through an extreme cold event.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: prolonged period below minus 30 degrees Celsius across the service area.

cards.label: Confirm the forecast duration and severity from weather services
Raise staffing, open the winter operations roster and brief all crews
Increase monitoring of shallow mains, storage levels and vulnerable areas
Issue customer guidance on dripping taps and protecting internal plumbing
Prioritize frozen service and burst responses by vulnerability and risk
Review demand, failures and costs daily until temperatures recover

tasks.explanation: Extreme cold is a campaign, not a shift. Early staffing, targeted monitoring and daily leadership review keep small freezes from becoming a backlog of burst services when the thaw arrives.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a capital program targeting frost driven failures.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program covering shallow mains, services and uninsulated chambers.

cards.label: Map repeat frost failures against burial depth and soil data
Group problem streets and services into correction areas
Choose corrections by site, from deepening to insulation or rerouting
Sequence areas by failure history and coordination with road programs
Deliver corrections in the summer construction season
Compare failure rates in corrected areas over the following winters

tasks.explanation: Frost corrections compete for summer construction capacity, so areas are grouped and sequenced by evidence. Comparing failure rates over following winters proves the program is fixing frost, not just spending on it.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing authorized bleed water use during winter.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: policy for services and mains run to prevent freezing, with volume accounting.

cards.label: Set the criteria for authorizing a bleed, including depth and freeze history
Record each authorized bleed with its flow setting and start date
Total bleed volumes monthly and include them honestly in the water balance
Review each bleed at set intervals and stop it when risk has passed
Flag repeat bleed sites for permanent correction in the capital program
Report total winter bleed volume and cost in the spring review

tasks.explanation: Bleeds prevent freezes but waste treated water, so they are authorized, metered by setting and time limited. Repeat sites are a capital list in disguise, and honest accounting keeps the loss visible.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a seasonal staffing and fatigue management plan for winter operations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plan covering rosters, overtime limits, contractor support and rest rules.

cards.label: Forecast winter workload from failure history and the frost outlook
Build rosters that cover peak periods without relying on unlimited overtime
Set fatigue limits and rest rules for extended cold events
Arrange contractor and mutual aid support for surge periods
Brief all staff on the roster, call out order and rest rules before winter
Review hours and fatigue reports weekly during the cold season

tasks.explanation: Winter failures cluster exactly when staff are most tired. Rosters built on forecast workload, with enforced rest rules, protect both the crews and the quality of emergency work.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a winter resilience audit of storage and pump stations.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: audit of heating, backup power, access and freeze protection at all sites.

cards.label: List every site and its freeze sensitive equipment and access risks
Inspect heating, insulation, backup power and alarm coverage at each site
Test backup power under load and confirm fuel reserves for extended outages
Grade deficiencies by the risk of losing the site in extreme cold
Complete the highest risk corrections before the cold season
Retest corrected sites and record the audit in the winter readiness file

tasks.explanation: A pump station lost to a failed heater in extreme cold is a preventable outage. Testing backup power under load, not just starting it, and grading corrections by risk focuses the pre winter work.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for planning for the spring thaw break surge.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: readiness plan for the surge of breaks and frozen services found at thaw.

cards.label: Analyse past thaw periods for break numbers, timing and locations
Pre position repair materials and fittings for the expected failure types
Set surge rosters and contractor call off arrangements for the thaw window
Prepare customer messages explaining thaw failures and reporting routes
Monitor frost depth and temperature trends to time the surge start
Stand down surge arrangements in stages as failure rates return to normal

tasks.explanation: The thaw surge is predictable in timing if not in detail. Materials, rosters and messages prepared in advance, triggered by frost and temperature monitoring, turn a yearly crisis into a managed season.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for updating distribution design standards for cold climate performance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: standards covering burial depth, insulation, chamber design and materials.

cards.label: Review failure records for design related frost and cold damage
Compare current standards with the frost depth data for the service area
Draft revised depth, insulation and material requirements by soil and area
Test the draft standards for cost impact on typical projects
Approve the standards and apply them to all new designs from a set date
Review standard performance after three winters of new construction

tasks.explanation: Design standards are where winter performance is decided for decades. Grounding revisions in local frost data and failure records, then reviewing new construction after three winters, closes the design loop.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading winter supply support for a remote northern community system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: support arrangement where the utility advises a small remote system through winter.

cards.label: Agree the support scope, decision authority and contact routine with the community
Review the system winter risks, from intake freezing to fuel and parts access
Confirm critical spares and chemicals are on site before freeze up
Set a scheduled check in routine through the winter with clear escalation routes
Respond to issues with remote guidance first and travel only when required and safe
Review the winter jointly in spring and update the support plan

tasks.explanation: Remote winter support succeeds on preparation before freeze up, because travel in deep winter is slow and hazardous. Scheduled check ins with clear escalation keep small problems from becoming supply failures.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the board review of winter operations performance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual review covering failures, costs, customer impact and readiness spending.

cards.label: Compile winter failure, response, bleed and cost data against the strategy standards
Compare performance with the previous three winters on the same measures
Identify the largest avoidable costs and the corrections that would remove them
Report readiness spending against the failures it prevented where evidence allows
Present recommended strategy and budget changes for the next winter
Record board decisions and carry them into the winter readiness plan

tasks.explanation: Comparing winters on the same measures separates weather luck from management performance. Presenting avoidable costs with their corrections gives the board a spending decision, not just a weather report.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading the annual regulatory reporting cycle for distribution.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: reporting required under provincial drinking water requirements, plus the annual quality report.

cards.label: Confirm every report, deadline and data owner in a controlled reporting calendar
Collect and validate the data for each report from the systems of record
Have results reviewed by operations and quality leads before drafting
Draft reports accurately, stating non conformances plainly with corrective actions
Obtain senior sign off and submit each report by its deadline
Log submissions and carry corrective actions into the compliance tracker

tasks.explanation: Regulatory credibility is built by stating non conformances plainly and fixing them visibly. A controlled calendar with named data owners stops deadline risk concentrating on one person.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for preparing the utility for a provincial drinking water inspection.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: readiness across records, facilities, sampling and staff knowledge.

cards.label: Review the last inspection report and confirm every past action is closed
Audit current records against the areas inspectors routinely examine
Walk facilities and sampling points to correct housekeeping and access issues
Brief staff on inspection conduct, honesty and where records are found
Host the inspection with a knowledgeable guide and full record access
Respond to findings with a corrective plan inside the required timeline

tasks.explanation: Inspection readiness is mostly the discipline of closing past actions and keeping records findable. Staff briefed to be honest and helpful make the inspection a verification, not an investigation.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for the annual management review of the quality management system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: review covering operational plan, audit results, incidents and improvement for distribution.

cards.label: Compile audit findings, incident reviews and performance results for the year
Assess whether the operational plan still matches the system risks and assets
Review the status of improvement actions set at the previous review
Set new improvement priorities with owners and resources for the coming year
Record the review decisions and communicate them to all affected staff
Verify at mid year that the review actions are progressing as recorded

tasks.explanation: Management review is where the quality system is steered, not just described. Checking last year actions before setting new ones prevents the review becoming an annual ritual of fresh promises.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a succession strategy for critical distribution roles.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: roles covering senior operators, control room, quality and emergency leads.

cards.label: Identify roles where one departure would remove critical knowledge or authority
Document the essential knowledge, licences and relationships for each role
Name and develop at least one ready successor for each critical role
Use acting assignments and project leadership to test readiness
Capture expert knowledge in procedures and mentoring before retirements
Review succession coverage annually and report gaps to leadership

tasks.explanation: Succession is tested by acting assignments, not by names on a chart. Capturing knowledge before retirement dates, while the expert can still correct the record, is the work that makes succession real.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a competency and certification strategy for distribution staff.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy aligning certification levels, training and role requirements across the utility.

cards.label: Map every role to the certification and competencies it requires
Compare current staff qualifications with the map to find gaps and surpluses
Build development plans that close gaps through training, rotation and mentoring
Schedule certification preparation so exam readiness matches vacancy risk
Track competency coverage by team and report it with staffing reports
Review the strategy when roles, technology or requirements change

tasks.explanation: A role by role map turns certification from individual ambition into utility capability. Tracking coverage by team shows leadership where a single absence would leave a shift unqualified.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for structuring a major decision where the evidence is uncertain.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: senior decision such as committing to a new supply source with incomplete data.

cards.label: State the decision, the deadline and what depends on it in writing
Separate what is known, what is assumed and what is unknown
Develop options that keep future choices open where the cost of waiting is low
Set the evidence that would change the decision and a date to check for it
Decide, record the reasoning and the uncertainties accepted
Review the decision when the check date arrives or new evidence appears

tasks.explanation: Writing down what is unknown stops assumptions hardening into facts. Options that preserve choice, plus a set date to revisit the evidence, let leaders decide now without pretending to certainty.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing selection of a major new operational technology.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: selection such as a new network monitoring platform for the whole utility.

cards.label: Define the operational problems the technology must solve and the success measures
Scan the market and shortlist options that meet the mandatory requirements
Pilot the leading options in real operations with the staff who will use them
Evaluate total cost, integration effort, supplier strength and pilot results
Select and contract with performance measures and exit terms included
Review realized benefits one year after full implementation

tasks.explanation: Technology chosen by the people who must use it, piloted in real operations, fails less often. Contracted performance measures and a one year benefits review stop selection being the end of accountability.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for negotiating an intermunicipal water service agreement.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: agreement for one municipality to supply treated water to a neighbouring community.

cards.label: Define the service required, volumes, quality duties and term under discussion
Model the effect of the added demand on capacity, storage and water age
Cost the service fully, including capacity reserved and renewal contributions
Negotiate terms covering price review, quality duties, emergencies and exit
Obtain approvals from both councils or boards on the recorded terms
Operate the agreement with joint performance reporting and an annual review

tasks.explanation: Reserved capacity is a real cost even when water is not flowing, so it is priced openly. Joint reporting and annual review keep the agreement a working relationship rather than a dormant contract.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for producing the annual public accountability report for the utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: public report covering quality, loss, investment, service and environmental performance.

cards.label: Select the performance areas the public has a right to judge the utility on
Present results honestly, including targets missed and the reasons
Explain major investments in terms of the service they bought
Publish the report in accessible formats and promote it to customers
Invite questions and answer them at a public session or in writing
Carry public feedback into the next year priorities and say so in the report

tasks.explanation: Accountability means publishing missed targets with reasons, not only successes. Closing the loop by showing where public feedback changed priorities is what makes the next report credible.

tasks.prompt: A benchmarking panel ranks a small Saskatchewan utility worst in its peer group on infrastructure leakage index, yet its absolute leakage volume is the lowest of the group.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional peer review of six prairie utilities. Leakage, pressure, and connection data were submitted on a common template.

evidence.label: The utility has the lowest real loss in cubic metres per day of all six utilities.
It also has the highest average pressure and the shortest mains per connection in the group.
Its unavoidable annual real loss allowance is small because mains length and connection count are small.
When loss is ranked per connection instead of by the index, the utility ranks second best.
A paired utility with triple the leakage volume scores a better index because its allowance is much larger.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The index ranking is misleading here, because the small allowance denominator inflates the index despite low absolute loss
The utility truly leaks more than every peer and the volume figures must be wrong
High pressure alone proves this utility has the worst leakage control in the group
The paired utility with triple the volume is clearly the better performer on leakage

inference.explanation: The index divides actual loss by an allowance that is tiny for this small, short main system, so a low volume still scores poorly. Volume and per connection rankings both contradict a worst performer reading.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Report both the index and absolute loss per connection to the board, and set the loss target in volume terms
Adopt the highest cost leakage program in the peer group to fix the index rank
Lower pressure across the whole system until the index matches the peer median

nextClue.explanation: Dual reporting stops a ratio artifact from driving spending while the real volume stays visible.

clueText.nc-a: Board reporting on both bases shows the utility second best on volume with a modest, targeted program.
clueText.nc-b: The costliest program targets a ranking, not the measured small volume of water actually lost.
clueText.nc-c: Pressure is one factor in the allowance, and a blanket cut risks service levels to chase an index.

tasks.prompt: A British Columbia utility must set its economic leakage target: each added survey round costs more while the water it saves is worth less at the margin.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional interior utility with a costed leakage program. Marginal costs and savings were tracked round by round.

evidence.label: Round one of detection saved water worth four times the round cost.
Round two saved water worth about the round cost.
Round three is projected to save water worth half the round cost, using the same unit rates.
The value of saved water includes treatment, pumping energy, and deferred capacity value.
Break frequency and night flow both level off after round two in the trial district.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Leakage should be driven to zero because any saved water has value
The economic level sits near round two, where marginal saving value meets marginal program cost
Round one results prove every further round will pay for itself four times over
Detection should stop entirely because round three does not pay

inference.explanation: Marginal value falls round by round and crosses program cost near round two, which defines the economic level. Zero leakage ignores rising marginal cost, and stopping entirely abandons a round that still pays.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Expand to monthly city wide surveys to push leakage toward zero
Hold the program at the round two intensity and reprice the marginal balance each year
Cancel the detection program and rely on break repairs only

nextClue.explanation: Holding at the economic level and repricing yearly keeps the program where evidence says it pays.

clueText.nc-a: Monthly surveys cost far more than the marginal water they could save past round two.
clueText.nc-b: Annual repricing confirms the program stays at the break even intensity as values change.
clueText.nc-c: Cancelling detection gives up the round one and two savings the trial measured.

tasks.prompt: An Alberta utility group reports apparent loss far above real loss at every member system, and leadership must decide whether to fund meter fleets or mains first.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional group of five Alberta systems with a shared component audit. Meter testing and night flow analysis used common methods.

evidence.label: Component audits put apparent loss at 14 to 19 percent of supply at all five systems.
Real loss from night flow analysis is 6 to 9 percent at all five systems.
Customer meter test benches show small meters under registering by 11 percent on average at low flows.
Billing audits found a large block of estimated reads carried for over a year at each system.
Step tests find no district with leakage matching the apparent loss scale.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Mains renewal should lead because all loss is leakage
Meter error is too small to matter at these percentages
Apparent loss dominates the measured balance, so metering and billing accuracy should lead the strategy
Both components are equal, so funding should split evenly

inference.explanation: Tested meter error and estimated reads explain an apparent component roughly double the real component at every system, and step tests exclude leakage at that scale. An even split ignores a two to one measured difference.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Fund mains renewal first across all five systems
Split the budget evenly between meters and mains this year
Fund the meter fleet and billing accuracy program first, and keep detection at maintenance scale

nextClue.explanation: Leading with the dominant measured component removes the most loss per dollar across the group.

clueText.nc-a: Renewal first spends on the smaller component while the larger one is already located in metering.
clueText.nc-b: Even splitting ignores the component audit the group paid to produce.
clueText.nc-c: After the metering program, apparent loss falls by more than half at the first two systems.

tasks.prompt: Two Manitoba utilities report the same leakage per kilometre, but a strategy review finds their loss problems are not the same problem at all.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional paired review of two similar sized systems. Pressure, night flow, and break data were normalized before comparison.

evidence.label: Utility A averages 420 kPa zone pressure, Utility B averages 260 kPa.
Leakage per kilometre is equal, but Utility A night flow falls 40 percent in a pressure reduction trial.
Utility B night flow barely changes in the same trial.
Utility B breaks cluster on one deteriorated cast iron cohort, Utility A breaks are spread evenly.
Both systems have similar soil, age mix overall, and connection density.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Both utilities need the same renewal program because leakage per kilometre matches
Utility B should cut pressure first because its pressure is lower
Utility A leakage is mostly background and joint loss that pressure cannot affect
Utility A is pressure driven and suits pressure management, while Utility B is condition driven and suits targeted renewal

inference.explanation: The pressure trial separates the two systems directly: A responds strongly and B does not, and B break pattern points to one failing cohort. Equal per kilometre figures hide opposite drivers.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Pilot pressure management in Utility A and schedule cohort renewal in Utility B, each with its own loss target
Apply one shared program and one shared target to both utilities
Cut pressure in Utility B first and renew Utility A first

nextClue.explanation: Matching each tool to its proven driver is the only plan the paired trial supports.

clueText.nc-a: Separate pilots cut loss in both systems within a year, each by its own mechanism.
clueText.nc-b: A shared program would apply each tool where the trial showed it does not work.
clueText.nc-c: Reversing the tools repeats the mismatch the review was done to find.

tasks.prompt: A utility in Saskatchewan presents a precise looking loss figure to its board, but a data validity review grades most audit inputs as estimates.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional board audit review. Each audit input was graded from measured to estimated by an external reviewer.

evidence.label: Production meters are calibrated and graded high validity.
Customer consumption includes 30 percent estimated reads in the audit year.
Unbilled authorized use is a flat allowance with no metering or logs behind it.
Two district flows are modelled, not metered, for the audit year.
The reported loss is stated to one decimal place with no range.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The audit should be reported as a range with a validity grade, and input metering fixed before targets are set
The loss figure is decision ready because production metering is strong
The decimal place is justified because the workbook calculates it
Estimated reads do not affect a water balance at all

inference.explanation: Three of the balance inputs are estimates or models, so a single precise figure overstates what the data support. Production accuracy alone cannot carry the whole balance.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Set a firm loss reduction target on the current figure this year
Meter the modelled districts and unbilled uses, then report loss as a graded range until inputs improve
Report the figure as is, since the board expects one number

nextClue.explanation: Fixing the weakest inputs first is what makes the next audit able to carry a target.

clueText.nc-a: A firm target on estimated inputs rewards or punishes estimation error, not field performance.
clueText.nc-b: With districts metered, the next audit range narrows by more than half.
clueText.nc-c: One ungraded number hides exactly the uncertainty the review documented.

tasks.prompt: A benchmarking study compares minimum night flow across four western utilities, and the raw league table puts the densest city last.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional four utility benchmark with a common night flow method. Density, pressure, and household use data were collected for normalization.

evidence.label: Raw night flow per kilometre is highest in the densest city and lowest in the rural system.
Night flow per connection reverses the ranking, putting the dense city near the top.
The dense city has four times the connections per kilometre of the rural system.
Legitimate night household use per connection is similar at all four utilities.
Average pressures differ by less than 10 percent across the four.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The dense city has the worst leakage because its per kilometre flow is highest
Per kilometre night flow misleads across different densities, and per connection comparison is the fair basis here
The rural system has the best leakage control on every basis
Night flow cannot be compared between utilities under any normalization

inference.explanation: With similar night use and pressure, the per kilometre gap tracks connection density, and the per connection basis reverses the rank. Density, not leakage, drives the raw table.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Rank utilities on raw per kilometre night flow in the annual report
Drop night flow benchmarking entirely
Benchmark on night flow per connection and publish density alongside every comparison

nextClue.explanation: A density aware basis keeps the benchmark useful instead of punishing compact systems.

clueText.nc-a: Raw per kilometre ranking would steer capital to the system the normalized data clear.
clueText.nc-b: The normalized comparison worked, so abandoning the measure wastes a valid tool.
clueText.nc-c: Per connection reporting shows all four utilities within a narrow band the next year.

tasks.prompt: A Yukon utility with one small crew must pick its first loss project: the audit points one way and a vendor proposal points the other.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional territorial utility with a completed component audit. A vendor proposal for a full meter changeout was received the same month.

evidence.label: The component audit puts real loss at 22 percent and apparent loss at 4 percent of supply.
Night flow is high in the oldest district and normal elsewhere.
Customer meter spot tests show accuracy within 3 percent across sizes.
The vendor proposal assumes 15 percent apparent loss with no test data for this system.
The crew can deliver one major project this construction season.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The meter changeout should lead because the vendor assumes large apparent loss
Both projects should run at half strength with the one crew
Real loss concentrated in the oldest district should lead, with detection and targeted repair this season
No project should run until apparent loss is proven zero

inference.explanation: The system own audit and meter tests contradict the vendor assumption, and night flow locates the dominant real loss. Splitting one crew across both dilutes the project the evidence supports.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Run detection and repair in the oldest district this season and retest the audit balance after
Sign the meter changeout on the vendor assumption
Split the crew between both projects at half strength

nextClue.explanation: One completed, located project beats two half finished ones for a single crew.

clueText.nc-a: District work cuts night flow by a third and real loss falls below 15 percent.
clueText.nc-b: The vendor figure was never measured on this system and its own tests contradict it.
clueText.nc-c: Half strength delivery left both projects unfinished in a comparable system trial.

tasks.prompt: A portfolio review of northern systems in the Northwest Territories shows every system loss spiking each winter, and a consultant blames failing mains across the portfolio.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional portfolio of six northern systems with freeze protection programs. Monthly production and bleed records were reviewed together.

evidence.label: Winter loss spikes match the months freeze protection bleed taps run at all six systems.
Bleed flow is supplied from treated storage and is not billed to any customer.
Break counts show no winter spike beyond normal seasonal variation at five of six systems.
Summer loss returns to a similar baseline at all six systems each year.
Only one system shows rising summer night flow, a separate pattern from the winter spikes.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: All six systems have mains failing every winter and recovering every summer
Bleed flow should be billed to the nearest customer to fix the audit
The one system with rising summer flow proves the consultant is right for all six
The winter spikes are unclassified bleed flow counted as loss, while one system has a separate real leakage trend to chase

inference.explanation: The spike is seasonal, metered as a program, and matched by flat break records, while the summer trend at one system is a different signal needing its own work. Mains do not fail and heal on a calendar.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Fund a portfolio wide winter renewal program on the consultant advice
Reclassify bleed flow as authorized unbilled use in every system audit, and open a separate leak investigation at the one rising system
Stop all bleed programs so winter audits improve

nextClue.explanation: Correct classification plus one targeted investigation matches both signals in the data.

clueText.nc-a: Portfolio renewal would spend on five systems whose spikes are accounting, not pipe failure.
clueText.nc-b: Reclassified audits show flat winter loss, and the single investigation finds a real trunk leak.
clueText.nc-c: Stopping bleed flow risks frozen services across the north to fix a classification error.

tasks.prompt: A growing Alberta city celebrates falling loss percentage for three years, but the senior operator warns council the celebration may be premature.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional city with rapid industrial growth. Audit volumes, not only percentages, were tabled for the three years.

evidence.label: Loss percentage fell from 24 to 17 percent over the three years.
Absolute real loss volume rose slightly each year over the same period.
Total supply rose 45 percent as two large industrial users connected.
Night flow per connection is unchanged over the three years.
No new detection or renewal program ran in the period.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The percentage fell because the denominator grew, while physical loss slightly worsened and still needs a program
