The loss program that never ran still delivered the improvement
Industrial growth should be refused because it distorts the percentage
Leakage truly fell because the percentage fell

inference.explanation: Volume and night flow both say physical loss did not fall, and no program ran that could have cut it. The percentage moved only because supply grew around a stable loss.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Report the percentage gain as a program success and hold the loss budget flat
Restate supply to exclude industrial use so the percentage looks stable
Report loss in volume and per connection terms to council and fund a detection program aimed at the rising volume

nextClue.explanation: Volume based reporting plus a real program addresses the loss the percentage hid.

clueText.nc-a: Claiming a success that never ran leaves a rising loss unfunded.
clueText.nc-b: Excluding real supply from the balance would falsify the audit to protect a ratio.
clueText.nc-c: Volume reporting shows the true trend, and year one detection cuts night flow measurably.

tasks.prompt: A regional utility in British Columbia must rank five member systems for one loss fund, and the loudest claim comes from the system with the weakest data.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional utility allocating a single loss fund. Each system submitted audit data graded for validity.

evidence.label: System A shows high loss on calibrated meters with district night flow confirmation.
System B shows the highest claimed loss, based entirely on estimated consumption and unmetered supply.
System C shows moderate loss with a completed step test locating it in two districts.
System D shows low loss on strong data and asks for no funding.
System E shows moderate claimed loss with no night flow or district data at all.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: System B should rank first because its claimed loss is highest
Systems A and C should lead because their losses are measured and located, while B and E first need metering to prove any claim
Funding should split equally across all five systems
System D should receive funds to keep the allocation fair

inference.explanation: Only A and C pair a loss figure with measurement and location, which is what repair funding needs. B highest claim rests on estimates at both ends of its balance.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Fund located work in A and C, and fund metering in B and E as the first step toward future claims
Fund B first on its claimed figure
Split the fund equally across the five systems

nextClue.explanation: Funding proof first and work where loss is located gets both fairness and results.

clueText.nc-a: A and C cut measured loss in year one, and B metering shows its true loss is half the claim.
clueText.nc-b: Funding an unmeasured claim first would spend repair money where no loss is located.
clueText.nc-c: Equal splits ignore both need and evidence strength across the five systems.

tasks.prompt: A utility leadership team in Saskatchewan reviews its performance dashboard and finds three headline indicators pointing the wrong way at once.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional dashboard review at utility scale. Indicator definitions were audited against the underlying operational records.

evidence.label: Loss percentage improved while absolute loss volume worsened, on growing supply.
Energy per megalitre worsened while lift corrected efficiency improved, on a new high zone coming into service.
Breaks per kilometre worsened while total breaks fell, after a low density annexation.
All three underlying operational trends are verified in the source records.
Staff bonuses were proposed against the three headline indicators as written.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The utility is failing on all three measures and bonuses should be denied
Indicators should be chosen to make performance look stable
Source records must be wrong where they contradict the dashboard
All three headlines are denominator and mix effects, so the dashboard needs volume, corrected, and split indicators before it steers pay or programs

inference.explanation: Each headline reverses its own verified source trend through a named mix or denominator effect, the same failure in three costumes. Paying or programming against them would reward and punish arithmetic, not performance.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Rebuild the dashboard on absolute, corrected, and area split indicators and hold bonus decisions until it is adopted
Deny bonuses on the current headlines
Keep the dashboard and adjust the source records to match

nextClue.explanation: A rebuilt dashboard makes the next year decisions defensible to staff and board alike.

clueText.nc-a: The rebuilt dashboard aligns every headline with its verified source trend.
clueText.nc-b: Denying bonuses on false headlines punishes staff for annexation and growth arithmetic.
clueText.nc-c: Adjusting source records to match a dashboard would falsify the only true data in the case.

tasks.prompt: A prairie city capacity study forecasts a supply shortfall in eight years, but a senior review finds the forecast stacks two allowances for the same growth.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Saskatchewan city long range study. Forecast layers were audited line by line by the senior team.

evidence.label: The base forecast already includes full buildout of all approved subdivisions.
A separate growth allowance then adds the same subdivisions again as contingency growth.
A climate uplift is applied on top of a peak factor that already uses the hottest recent summer.
Removing the double counted layer moves the shortfall year from eight to beyond twenty years.
Actual demand has tracked the base forecast, not the stacked forecast, for five years.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The shortfall in eight years is real and a new source must start now
Actual demand tracking the base forecast is a coincidence with no meaning
The forecast double counts growth and climate allowances, so the shortfall is far later and staged planning fits
Contingency allowances should always be stacked without checking overlap

inference.explanation: Two layers count the same subdivisions, the climate uplift repeats the hot summer already in the peak factor, and actuals follow the unstacked base. The early shortfall is an artifact of stacking.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Start the new source project now on the eight year date
Restate the forecast on the base case with one transparent contingency, and set trigger points for the next source stage
Keep the stacked forecast because a larger safety margin is always better

nextClue.explanation: Trigger based staging protects supply without committing capital to a double counted date.

clueText.nc-a: Starting now commits major capital twenty years before the corrected need date.
clueText.nc-b: Restated planning holds the source stage until measured demand reaches the trigger.
clueText.nc-c: A hidden double count is not a safety margin, it is an error the review identified.

tasks.prompt: A British Columbia mountain utility weighs a new reservoir against a new well, and the binding constraint turns out to be neither average demand nor source yield.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility with two costed capacity options. Fire flow, peak hour, and storage tests were modelled for both options.

evidence.label: Average and maximum day demands are met by existing sources with either option.
The oldest neighbourhood fails required fire flow at peak hour with the well option alone.
The reservoir option restores fire flow in that neighbourhood by gravity head and storage.
Well yield testing is strong and exceeds the forecast maximum day need.
Storage in the system is the lowest per connection in its peer group.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The well should lead because its yield exceeds maximum day demand
Either option works because average demand is met
Fire flow can be ignored in a capacity strategy if yield is strong
Fire flow and storage, not source yield, bind this system, so the reservoir option addresses the real constraint

inference.explanation: Yield and average demand already pass, while fire flow fails and storage is peer low. The reservoir is the only option that fixes the failing tests.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Advance the well option on yield alone
Defer both options because average demand is met
Advance the reservoir option and record fire flow as the governing capacity criterion in the strategy

nextClue.explanation: Recording the governing criterion prevents the next study from re-arguing yield.

clueText.nc-a: The well leaves the documented fire flow failure exactly as modelled.
clueText.nc-b: Deferral leaves a known fire flow gap in place while demand is called met.
clueText.nc-c: Reservoir construction restores fire flow at peak hour in the oldest neighbourhood.

tasks.prompt: An Alberta city declares a large capacity surplus after per capita demand falls for a decade, and plans to sell the surplus to a neighbouring town.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional city reviewing a wholesale offer. Demand history and the cause of the per capita fall were examined before the decision.

evidence.label: Per capita residential demand fell steadily as fixtures and appliances improved.
Total city demand stayed flat because population grew at the same pace.
The city largest industrial user closed five years ago and its site is now listed for a water intensive reuse.
Firm source capacity exceeds current maximum day demand by 12 percent only.
The neighbour offer would commit 10 percent of firm capacity for thirty years.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The apparent surplus is mostly a closed plant and flat totals, so a thirty year commitment of nearly all spare firm capacity is imprudent
The surplus is large and the thirty year sale is safe
Per capita decline means total demand will keep falling regardless of growth
Industrial reuse can be ignored because the site has been empty five years

inference.explanation: Totals are flat, the spare margin is only 12 percent of firm capacity, and the offer consumes nearly all of it while a water intensive reuse is actively listed. The per capita trend does not create a sellable surplus.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Decline the long commitment, offer a shorter interruptible arrangement, and revisit after the industrial site future is known
Sign the thirty year sale on the per capita trend
Sell the full spare capacity and plan a new source only if reuse proceeds

nextClue.explanation: A short interruptible offer keeps the relationship without betting the whole margin.

clueText.nc-a: The interruptible arrangement serves the neighbour while the city margin stays intact.
clueText.nc-b: Thirty years at 10 percent leaves 2 percent margin against a listed industrial reuse.
clueText.nc-c: Planning a source after reuse proceeds starts years behind the demand it must serve.

tasks.prompt: A Manitoba lakeside town designs capacity from its annual average demand and is surprised every summer, so the strategy review rebuilds the design basis.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional resort town with strong seasonal population swing. Monthly and weekly demand records were reviewed over six summers.

evidence.label: Summer population is about three times the winter population for ten weeks.
Maximum week demand is 2.6 times the annual average week.
Storage sized on average demand empties during the peak week in four of six years.
Winter demand is met easily and the plant runs at low load for months.
A paired inland town with stable population shows no such seasonal pattern.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant is undersized for the whole year and needs a full capacity doubling
Design must be based on the seasonal peak week with storage and peaking capacity, not the annual average
Summer visitors should be restricted until average demand rises
The storage emptying is a metering artifact of the summer season

inference.explanation: The peak week ratio, repeated storage emptying, and the stable paired town all point to a design basis error, not a year round shortage. Average based sizing cannot serve a three to one seasonal swing.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Double plant capacity for year round operation
Rebuild the capacity plan on peak week demand and add seasonal storage and operating rules
Keep average based planning and accept summer storage emptying

nextClue.explanation: Peak week planning with seasonal rules matches capacity to the demand shape that exists.

clueText.nc-a: Doubling year round capacity overspends for a ten week pattern storage can carry.
clueText.nc-b: Peak week storage ends the summer emptying in the first season after the change.
clueText.nc-c: Accepting emptying accepts the failure the review documented four years in six.

tasks.prompt: A Saskatchewan utility claims its summer restriction program cut demand by 20 percent, but a paired comparison with an unrestricted neighbour tells a different story.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional evaluation of a two year restriction program. A similar neighbouring system with no restrictions served as the comparison.

evidence.label: Restricted city summer demand fell 20 percent in the program year.
The unrestricted neighbour summer demand fell 18 percent the same year.
The program year was the wettest and coolest summer in a decade in both cities.
In the following dry summer, restricted city demand returned to its historic level.
Outdoor use is the dominant summer demand in both cities.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Restrictions caused the full 20 percent reduction
The neighbour comparison is invalid because the cities differ in size
Weather explains most of the fall in both cities, so the program effect is small and unproven on this evidence
The dry summer rebound proves restrictions increased demand

inference.explanation: Both cities fell almost equally in a record wet cool summer and the restricted city rebounded fully in a dry year, which is a weather signature, not a program signature. Size difference does not erase an 18 versus 20 percent match.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Credit the full 20 percent as firm savings in the capacity plan
Cancel all restrictions because the evaluation was imperfect
Evaluate the program over a dry year with the neighbour comparison kept, before crediting savings in the capacity plan

nextClue.explanation: A dry year paired test is the honest way to size any real program effect.

clueText.nc-a: Crediting 20 percent firm would underbuild capacity on a weather artifact.
clueText.nc-b: Cancelling discards a program whose true, smaller effect was never measured.
clueText.nc-c: The dry year test shows a small real effect that can be credited with confidence.

tasks.prompt: An Alberta growth corridor strategy counts every proposed subdivision at full buildout in five years, and servicing costs explode on paper.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional corridor servicing strategy. Developer phasing records for the past decade were compared with proposal counts.

evidence.label: Over the past decade, approved subdivisions in the corridor reached full buildout in an average of fourteen years.
Only half of proposed subdivisions in any five year window actually started construction.
The strategy assumes all proposed areas at full buildout within five years.
Servicing sized on that assumption requires two major trunk projects immediately.
Phased servicing tied to actual starts defers one trunk project by about a decade in the model.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: All proposed areas should be serviced at once because approval equals buildout
Trunk projects should be sized for the fastest imaginable buildout
Growth should be refused until all trunk capacity is built
Phasing assumptions should follow the decade of observed starts and buildout pace, with triggers for acceleration

inference.explanation: A decade of starts and buildout pace directly contradicts the five year full buildout assumption, and phasing on observed behaviour defers a trunk by a decade. Approval has never equalled buildout in this corridor.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Adopt phased servicing with start based triggers and review the pace assumption every two years
Build both trunk projects now on the five year assumption
Freeze all corridor approvals until both trunks are complete

nextClue.explanation: Trigger based phasing builds capacity as real starts prove the need.

clueText.nc-a: Phased triggers hold servicing in step with starts through the next review cycle.
clueText.nc-b: Building both now strands capital if the decade pace repeats, as it has for ten years.
clueText.nc-c: A freeze punishes real starts for a forecasting assumption the records refute.

tasks.prompt: A British Columbia city finds its maximum day factor falling for fifteen years, and the treatment and storage expansion case changes with it.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional city reviewing its design factors. Fifteen years of average and maximum day records were trended.

evidence.label: The maximum day to average day ratio fell from 2.1 to 1.5 over fifteen years.
Outdoor irrigation share fell as lot sizes shrank and pricing changed.
The expansion design still uses the historic 2.1 factor.
Using the current 1.5 factor, existing capacity serves the forecast horizon without expansion.
A sensitivity check at 1.7 still defers expansion beyond fifteen years.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The design factor should be updated to the measured trend with a sensitivity margin, deferring the expansion
The historic 2.1 factor must be kept because it was used before
The falling factor is a data error because ratios do not change
Expansion is needed now because the old factor says so

inference.explanation: Fifteen years of records, a clear demand cause, and a sensitivity case all support the lower factor. Keeping 2.1 designs for a demand pattern that no longer exists.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Proceed with the expansion on the historic factor
Update the design factor with the sensitivity margin and set a monitoring trigger if the ratio rises again
Adopt the lowest single year ratio as the new design factor

nextClue.explanation: An updated factor plus a rise trigger keeps the plan both lean and safe.

clueText.nc-a: Expanding on the old factor builds capacity the measured demand does not need.
clueText.nc-b: Monitoring confirms the ratio stays near the trend and the expansion stays deferred.
clueText.nc-c: A single low year is as unrepresentative as the stale historic factor.

tasks.prompt: A regional system in Manitoba serves five towns from one source, and the shared capacity plan fails because it treats the five growth paths as one.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional system capacity review. Town by town growth and demand records were separated for the first time.

evidence.label: One town grows at 3 percent a year near a new highway interchange.
Two towns are flat and one is slowly shrinking.
The shared plan applies one blended growth rate to all five towns.
Local storage and mains in the growing town reach limits years before the shared source does.
The shrinking town shows rising per connection costs under the blended plan.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The blended plan is fair because all towns share one source
Each town needs its own growth path in the plan, with local works staged for the growing town and shared source capacity rechecked on the sum
The growing town should be capped to fit the blended plan
The shrinking town proves the whole region needs no capacity work

inference.explanation: The blended rate hides a fast growing town whose local limits bind first and overstates need elsewhere. Summing separate paths is both fairer and more accurate than one blended rate.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Keep the blended plan and treat all towns alike
Cap growth in the growing town to protect the blended plan
Rebuild the plan town by town and stage the growing town local works first

nextClue.explanation: Town by town staging puts the first dollar where the first limit actually binds.

clueText.nc-a: The blended plan was the method that produced the failure under review.
clueText.nc-b: Capping a growing town to fit a spreadsheet exports the planning error to residents.
clueText.nc-c: The rebuilt plan stages local works in time and rebalances regional costs fairly.

tasks.prompt: A northern Manitoba utility discovers its true peak day now falls in January, not July, and its capacity strategy was written for a summer peak system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional northern utility with year round demand logging. Winter protection practices and summer use were compared over five years.

evidence.label: January demand has exceeded July demand in three of the last five years.
Winter bleed taps and customer drip protection run continuously during cold snaps.
Cold snap demand rises within hours of extreme cold warnings and falls as temperatures ease.
Summer irrigation is minor because the growing season is short.
Source and storage were sized and operated for a July peak with a winter low period.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: July remains the design peak because that is the normal pattern in Canada
January peaks are meter errors caused by cold weather
The system peak has shifted to winter freeze protection demand, and capacity and operations must be planned for the cold snap case
Bleed taps should be banned so the July design basis becomes true again

inference.explanation: Three years of January exceedance, a clear cold snap mechanism, and minor summer use make the winter peak real. A design basis is a measurement, not a tradition.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Rewrite the capacity basis around the cold snap peak and add winter operating and storage rules
Keep the July basis and treat January exceedances as anomalies
Ban bleed taps across the system this winter

nextClue.explanation: A cold snap basis with winter rules plans for the peak that actually occurs.

clueText.nc-a: The rewritten basis sizes the next storage stage for the January case and ends the exceedances.
clueText.nc-b: Anomaly treatment failed three times in five years on the same pattern.
clueText.nc-c: Banning taps would freeze services system wide to defend an outdated design basis.
